title: The king who lived afraid
hookLine: Kamsa falls in his own arena, and reaches Krishna through fear
carry: a mind fixed on krishna reaches him

lines: THE CROWD SAYS, THIS IS WRONG.
cards: The women in the stands aren't happy. Down on the wrestling ground, Kamsa's champion Chanura has squared off against Krishna, and his partner Mushtika against Balarama: giants against two boys from the pastures.
The Bhagavata lets us hear the crowd. This is wrong, the women tell each other. It's no fair match.
Whoever allowed it shares the blame. And the cowherd girls of Vraja were lucky, they say, to see him every day.

teach.b: The fight goes hold for hold, then turns. Krishna brings down Chanura, Balarama brings down Mushtika, and the other wrestlers fall or run. Kamsa orders the music stopped.
He shouts for the boys to be driven out, and for Vasudeva and his own father Ugrasena to be killed.

teach.h: HE WAS NEVER NOT THINKING OF HIM.
teach.b: Before he finishes, Krishna is on the platform. Kamsa reaches for his sword. Krishna catches him by the hair, pulls him down into the arena, and it's over.

Then the Bhagavata says something striking. All his life, eating, drinking, walking, sleeping, Kamsa thought of Krishna, out of fear. And because his mind was so fixed on him, the text says, he reached him in the end.
It's the frame from the rasa lila: what matters is where the mind is turned, even by terror. Hindus take that seriously in daily life.
It's why they keep God's name close: chanting it on beads, singing it, saying it when they're scared, and saying Rama's or Krishna's name beside someone who is dying.
In the Gita, Krishna says whatever a person remembers at the end, that is where they go. Kamsa remembered Krishna by accident, out of dread. Devotees try to do it on purpose, out of love.
Kamsa's wives come weeping, and Krishna comforts them and sees the funeral rites done. Then he frees his parents, Vasudeva and Devaki, and bows at their feet.
So the story of his childhood closes where it began: a birth in a prison cell, and now the cell door open, and a son kneeling before his mother.

how: Kamsa's death and the freeing of Devaki and Vasudeva are retold from the Bhagavata, and Kamsa's defeat is acted out in festival performances in the Mathura area.

o: Kamsa's escape from Mathura on the night of the fight
a festival held each year to remember Kamsa's rule
the end of King Kamsa, pulled down in his own arena

games.q: the end of Kamsa — tap the pairs.

s: the crowd cheers the match between the wrestlers and the boys
the women in the stands say it's wrong, no fair match at all.
the text says Kamsa reached Krishna through fear
eating, drinking, walking, sleeping, he thought of Krishna out of fear, and that fixed mind reached him.
the story ends with a victory feast
Krishna comforts Kamsa's wives, sees to the funeral rites, and goes to free his parents.

games.q: you're Krishna. Kamsa is dead, and his wives come weeping into the arena. what do you do?
o: comfort them and see that the funeral rites are done.
send them out of the city.
games.why: the Bhagavata says Krishna consoles Kamsa's wives and arranges his funeral rites, before going to free his parents.

practice: Hindus call this nama japa, repeating the name. Bring to mind one small fear you've been carrying. Then, with each slow breath, say one name of God softly: Krishna, or Rama, or the name you use.
Let the fear and the name sit together, the way they did in Kamsa, but turned toward love. If you don't pray, choose one steady word and let it carry each breath.

wordCard.voice: Kamsa's death. The king who spent his life afraid of Krishna, pulled down in his own arena, and reaching him, the text says, through his fear.

orig.note: Sanskrit: fear. The text says Kamsa's fear kept his mind on Krishna all his life.

carryVoice: Your line: a mind fixed on Krishna reaches him. Kamsa got there through fear; devotees go by love. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 10.44, the wrestling match, the women's protest, Kamsa's death, his attainment through fear, the comforting of his wives, and the freeing of Vasudeva and Devaki
Bhagavata Purana 10.29, Shuka's answer to Parikshit (minds fixed on Krishna through any feeling)
Bhagavad Gita 8.6, whatever a person remembers at the end, to that they go
